What the Maricopa County Recorder does

Land records in the county live at the Maricopa County Recorder's Office, which also handles voter registration and mail voting. It reports more than 52 million recorded documents and more than 2.6 million eligible voters. A seller deals with two kinds of paper here: the deed that passes title to the buyer, and the lender's release when the old loan is paid off.

Staff won't advise on legal questions, fill in forms for you or notarize anything. Unsure which form you need? Ask a title company, estate planner or attorney. Call the recording line at 602-506-3535 for process questions.

With 4,420,568 residents in the 2020 census, Maricopa is Arizona's largest county, covering fifteen cities and ten towns. One downtown office takes recordings for all of them, whether the house is in Phoenix, Gila Bend or Wickenburg.

Where and how to record a deed

Three routes exist: walk in, mail it, or submit electronically. Whatever you choose, send an original or a certified copy issued by a government agency. Walk-ins go to Suite 200 at 301 W Jefferson St, Phoenix, AZ 85003, weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. except holidays. No appointment is required, and you leave with your original in hand.

  • Counter: pay with cash, card or a check made out to Maricopa County Recorder.
  • Mail: address the envelope to Attn. Copy Desk and enclose a check, cashier's check or money order. Expect the recorded original back at your return address after 2 to 4 weeks. Same-day recording of mailed items isn't promised.
  • Electronic: digital accounts are meant for high-volume filers. If you have one document, a third-party submitter can send it for you.

In practice the title or escrow company files the deed at closing, so you rarely visit. Your part is signing the deed and its affidavit correctly ahead of closing day.

Plan the order of events this way: you sign at the title company, the buyer's funds arrive, and the deed is submitted for recording. If a signature is missing or a name is misspelled, recording stalls and closing can slip, so ask the title officer to review the deed with you a few days early, so there is time to fix it.

Recording fees

A.R.S. 11-475 sets the usual charge at $30 for each document, however many pages it runs. Other charges are below.

Most documents (not plats or surveys)$30

Fees are collected before recording, so a mailed deed has to arrive with the correct total. Your title company can tell you about other charges that may show on your settlement statement.

What a Maricopa County deed must include

Every deed carries one of two things: an Affidavit of Property Value, or an exemption code written on the deed. The affidavit reports the price and date of the sale plus other deal terms. Staff can't choose an exemption code for you.

A.R.S. 11-1133 governs it. Both parties, or their agents, sign the Department of Revenue form, and it applies to deeds and to contracts of sale. The form collects:

  • Contact details for the buyer and the seller
  • Who should receive the tax statement, and where
  • Legal description, street address and assessor's parcel number
  • Sale date, total consideration, cash down and financing type
  • A yes or no on whether personal property is 5% or more of the price
  • How the parties are related and whether the buyer will live in the house or rent it out

An incomplete affidavit means the recorder must turn the deed away, unless an exemption is noted on it. Layout of the document itself, such as caption and margins, follows A.R.S. 11-480 and the office's form requirements page.

How recording connects to property tax

Once the deed is recorded, the Assessor knows the new owner and the mailing address for the tax statement. The Treasurer bills that person from then on. A fall sale raises one question: was the first half paid? It comes due October 1, and late status starts after 5:00 p.m. on November 1, which in 2026 shifted to November 2 because the first was a Sunday. Pay the whole year by December 31 and no interest applies.

The tax also works as a lien. A.R.S. 42-17153 has it taking hold each January 1, ahead of most other claims on the house. Expect the title company to pay anything unpaid out of your sale proceeds. Call the Maricopa County Treasurer at 602-506-8511 for what is owed.

A free alert service called Maricopa Title Alert, run through the Recorder's Office and linked from the Assessor's site, notifies you when a document is registered against your property. Heirs and out-of-state owners find it handy. One bill from the Treasurer spans more than 1,800 tax districts: cities, schools, community colleges and special districts. Money left over after a foreclosure sale is posted on the Treasurer's site under A.R.S. 33-812.

Checklist before recording day

Run through these before anything goes to the counter.

  • Spelling of every name, including a trust, matches how title is held.
  • Legal description and parcel number copy the previous deed.
  • The affidavit is signed, or the exemption code appears on the deed.
  • You have a signed original with the notary section filled in.
  • Your return address sits at the upper left of page one.
  • The check covers $30 for every document in the stack.

Houses that pass through probate or a trust often need several deeds, and each one is charged separately. Have the title company list every document and give you one total.

A cash sale follows the same path: one deed, one affidavit, one fee. What it skips is the buyer's lender, so there is usually no new deed of trust to record. Your own old loan still ends with a release, though. After closing, ask the title company to confirm that release was recorded, and file the recorded copy with your sale papers.

If you do go to the counter yourself, bring the signed original deed, the completed affidavit or a written exemption code, a photo ID for any notary visit you arranged beforehand, and a payment method that covers the fee. Write down the recording number you are given. Later, if a buyer or lender asks for proof the deed went on record, that number lets title staff find it quickly.

Frequently asked questions

What does recording a deed cost in Maricopa County?

The usual price is $30 a document, whatever the page count. Plats and surveys run $24 for page one and $20 for each page after. Copies cost $1 a page and certifying a document costs $3.

Where do I take a deed to be recorded in Maricopa County?

Go to the downtown office, Suite 200 at 301 W Jefferson St in Phoenix. Hours are 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays, holidays excluded, and walk-ins need no appointment.

Is it okay to mail my deed to the Maricopa County Recorder?

Yes. Send the original to Attn. Copy Desk at the downtown address with a check, cashier's check or money order. It comes back to your return address within 2 to 4 weeks, and the office doesn't commit to recording on the day it arrives.

Do I need an Affidavit of Property Value to record a Maricopa County deed?

Yes, unless the deed shows an exemption code. A.R.S. 11-1133 sets the requirement, and the recorder has to refuse a deed that has neither a complete affidavit nor an exemption notation.

Can the Maricopa County Recorder's staff help me prepare a deed?

No. They don't give legal advice, help with forms or notarize. A title company, estate planner or attorney can prepare it, and 602-506-3535 reaches the recording line for process questions.

Where to record a Pima County deed

Land in Pima County is recorded at the Pima County Recorder's Office in Tucson, since state law makes the county of the property the place to file. Under A.R.S. 33-411, a later buyer or lender who paid value and had no notice isn't bound by an instrument that was never recorded in that county. Signing a deed doesn't finish the job; getting it onto the public record does.

Online, the Recorder offers record searches, e-recording, document pickup and a document services subscription. Maps to its two Tucson sites, 240 N Stone Avenue and 6920 E Broadway Boulevard, sit on the home page. Confirm current hours on the contact page before you go.

The office also runs elections and voter registration, so much of the site is about voting. For deed help, look for the Recording Fees, Recording Requirements and Recording FAQ links.

Recording fees

The usual charge is $30 for each instrument, set by A.R.S. 11-475 for papers the law requires or permits to be recorded. A government party that requests the recording pays $15. Section 11-475.01's amount is already inside the $30.

Price plays no part, since the county schedule lists only per-document charges. If you suspect another charge applies to your deed, check with the title company or the state Department of Revenue.

ChargeAmount

Payment methods

The office takes Visa, Mastercard, cash, checks and money orders, made payable to Pima County Recorder. Card payment is limited to the counter; phone and mail orders can't use one. Buying online adds a 2 percent card convenience fee.

Two rules sink many mailed packets.

  • Your name has to be pre-printed on the check.
  • Any check or money order must carry a date within 60 days of receipt.

No charge applies to military discharge papers under A.R.S. 11-465. A copy of a recorded document costs $0.25 per standard letter-size image, or $0.25 per digital document. Plats and survey maps are priced apart, at $24 for image one and $20 for each image after it.

What a deed must look like

Expect to supply a caption, original signatures, a legible original or copy and a legal description, along with an affidavit of property value unless the transfer is exempt. The layout rules sit on the Recording Requirements page and in A.R.S. 11-480; fall short and the counter may reject the document.

  • Title the instrument with a short caption, for example warranty deed.
  • Keep pages within 8 1/2 by 14 inches and type at ten point or larger.
  • Leave half-inch margins, and reserve the top two inches of page one for the recording stamp.
  • If you are modifying an earlier document, cite its recording date and its docket and page or sequence number.

The grantor has to sign the deed and acknowledge it before an authorized officer (A.R.S. 33-401). The County Attorney's Office has told Recorder staff not to give legal advice, so ask an attorney or title company which deed fits.

Why a Pima County deed comes back

Most returns trace to a short list of causes: no caption, margins that crowd the stamp area, a missing signature or acknowledgment, no affidavit or exemption notation, or a check that is undated, unprinted with your name or older than 60 days. A returned document costs $5, and a bounced check costs $25, on top of the delay.

Mailing adds $1 per document for processing, so a mailed deed with a check for $30 should include that extra dollar. Compare your packet with the list above before you seal the envelope, and ask your title company to look over the deed if the sale is on a tight schedule, because a rejected deed can push your closing date.

Photo ID for in-person recording

Walk-in customers recording a document show valid photo ID, as A.R.S. 11-472 requires. Acceptable choices are a state driver's license or ID card, a tribal enrollment card or other tribal ID, or any ID issued by a federal, state or local government.

The rule excludes documents brought by an escrow officer, a title insurer or agent, a chartered bank or credit union, a practicing member of the State Bar of Arizona, or a governmental entity. Most sellers never see it, because escrow files the deed. A recorder may jot down the ID's type, name and number but may not copy it, and that note isn't public.

Affidavit of property value and exemptions

Both buyer and seller sign this form, and it travels with the deed to the counter. Without a complete one, or an exemption notation, the Recorder must refuse the deed (A.R.S. 11-1133). The questions cover both names, the legal description, the sale date, the total consideration and owner-occupied versus rental use. Get the form from the Arizona Department of Revenue.

Certain transfers are excused by A.R.S. 11-1134, including these:

  • Gifts by deed.
  • Quitclaim deeds with no money exchanged.
  • Trustee's deeds after a deed of trust, and transfers made only to give or release security for a debt.
  • Homes passed for token consideration among spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, or siblings.
  • Beneficiary-deed transfers for token consideration.

If you claim an exemption, the Department of Revenue exemption letter and number must accompany the deed at recording. Your title company can verify the exact notation first.

Pima County housing context and next steps

Pima County is home to an estimated 1,074,685 people, with Tucson as seat and largest city. Housing units are 65.2 percent owner-occupied, and the median owner-occupied home is worth $319,700. Recording is identical across the county. Taxes are billed separately by the Pima County Treasurer at 240 N. Stone Avenue, which can quote an amount before closing.

Here is a workable order: check the deed's caption and margins, sign before a notary, finish the affidavit or note the exemption, then have the escrow or title office record it. Delivering it yourself? Bring photo ID and a $30 check payable to Pima County Recorder, dated within 60 days. Cash sales follow the same steps, minus a buyer's lender, so usually no loan document is recorded behind your deed.

Frequently asked questions

What does Pima County charge to record a deed?

$30 for each document, or $15 if a government agency requests it. Getting a document back for being improperly submitted costs $5, and a returned check costs $25.

Does Pima County tax the sale of a home when the deed is recorded?

Nothing on the Recorder's schedule depends on price. You pay the flat fee and file an affidavit of property value. Ask your title company or the Department of Revenue about any other charge.

Will Pima County Recorder staff help me complete a deed?

No, the County Attorney's Office has told them not to give legal advice. Use an attorney, escrow officer or title company to prepare it, and the Recorder reviews it against the form rules.

Is photo ID required to record in person in Pima County?

Yes, with exceptions for exempt submitters such as escrow offices, title insurers, banks, credit unions, State Bar members and government entities. The rule is A.R.S. 11-472.

What happens if a Pima County deed is never recorded?

A later buyer or lender who paid value without notice isn't bound by it (A.R.S. 33-411). The new owner is exposed, so record soon after closing.

Where to record a deed in Pinal County

Take a deed to the Pinal County Recorder's Office. Florence has the main office, and four others spread across the county. An instrument is recorded in Pinal County when the property sits in the county (A.R.S. 11-468). The same office also handles voter registration and early voting.

Mail goes to P.O. Box 848, Florence, AZ 85132. Don't expect a notary there. Staff also may not advise you on legal matters, help complete a form or pick a document type for you. Bring those questions to a title company, escrow officer or attorney.

Arizona law requires the grantor to sign the deed and acknowledge the signature before an authorized officer (A.R.S. 33-401). Get the deed notarized first, then send it on.

Recorder office locations and hours

Pinal County covers 5,374 square miles, so the Recorder runs five offices. Each is open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Florence (main)31 N Pinal Street, Building E, Florence, AZ 85132520-866-6830

The San Tan Valley office is off Bella Vista Road, just east of the Central Arizona College San Tan Campus. A seller in Maricopa or San Tan Valley can use the nearby office instead of driving to Florence.

What does it cost to record a deed in Pinal County?

The standard fee is $30 per document, and it falls to $15 when the United States, the state or a political subdivision asks for the recording. The Recording Fee Schedule took effect July 1, 2019 and follows the amendment to A.R.S. 11-475(A). The $30 already covers the affidavit of property value, extra indexing and the document and storage fee surcharge, and each recording fee includes $1 for postage to mail the document back.

  • Subdivision plats or maps (24 by 36 inches): $24, plus $20 for each additional sheet.
  • Survey and other maps (18 by 24 inches): $24, plus $20 for each additional sheet.
  • Plats and survey maps recorded at a government agency's request: $14 for the first sheet and $10 for each additional sheet.
  • Copies of recorded documents: $1 per page, with return postage included on mail requests, plus $3 per document for certification.

All of these are flat amounts. Nothing scales with the price of your house. Your title company can confirm that no other charge applies at closing.

How to submit a document

You can record in person at any of the five offices, send the original by mail, or use one of the trusted e-recording partners the county works with. For mail, enclose a check or money order for the amount on the fee schedule. For e-recording, call an office and ask for the partner list. The online document search reaches back to May 23, 1980, and any image you download is stamped as an unofficial copy.

In-person filers need photo ID under A.R.S. 11-472. Exceptions cover documents submitted by an escrow office, a title insurer or agent, a bank or credit union, an active State Bar of Arizona member, or a government entity. When escrow handles your closing, the escrow office files the deed and you skip the ID rule.

After a compliant document comes in, staff process it in four stages.

  • If the form is complete and the fees are paid, it becomes a permanent public record.
  • Data entry builds an index so the record can be found by name.
  • The document is optically scanned and microfilmed to meet state archival requirements.
  • The original goes back to the address typed on it.

Layout rules for the paper itself are in A.R.S. 11-480. Expect a caption, original signatures, pages no bigger than 8 1/2 by 14 inches, type of ten point or larger, and a blank two inch strip at the top of page one.

Transfer tax and the affidavit of property value

The fee schedule has no charge tied to the sale price, so there is no separate transfer tax to budget for. What the buyer and seller do owe the Recorder is an Affidavit of Real Property Value. A.R.S. 11-1133 and 11-1137(B) require both sides, or their agents, to complete and attest to it, and skipping it is a class 2 misdemeanor. County assessors and the Department of Revenue use the data to build tables for uniform valuation. One sale does not directly change the assessment or taxes on that property.

Sign and notarize the affidavit, then hand it in with the deed. Exempt transfers skip it. The exempt list in A.R.S. 11-1134 covers gifts, quitclaims given for no money, trustee's deeds, and transfers made for only nominal consideration between spouses, between parent and child, between grandparent and grandchild, between siblings, or under a beneficiary deed.

For an exempt transfer, write the statute number and exemption code on the face of the deed beneath the legal description, for example "A.R.S. 11-1134 B3." Don't complete the affidavit in that case.

Fixing or removing something on a recorded record

Nothing on the public record can be edited in place. A recorded transfer stands until a later recorded document changes it. The Recorder can't advise on how to hold title or how to take a decedent's name off a deed, so take those questions to a title company or an attorney.

  • To find easements on your property, read Schedule B of your title policy if the purchase closed through a title company. Otherwise search the Recorder's website using one party's name and an approximate recording date.
  • To have personal information removed from public records, read the Arizona statutes for the Recorder (A.R.S. 11-483), the Assessor and Treasurer (A.R.S. 11-484) and voter registration (A.R.S. 16-153).

Suspicious filings can be referred to the FBI or other law enforcement. Presenting a false instrument for recording is a class 6 felony under A.R.S. 39-161.

Recording steps in a typical Pinal County sale

Few sellers ever stand at the recording counter. Here is how a normal sale reaches the Recorder.

  • You sign the deed before a notary, and you and the buyer sign the Affidavit of Real Property Value unless the transfer is exempt.
  • The title or escrow company checks the caption, signatures and margins against A.R.S. 11-480.
  • That company delivers the package to the Recorder, pays the fee and receives the recorded original back.
  • You ask the title company for a copy of the recorded deed, which is your proof of the transfer date.

If you sell for cash without a lender, the sequence is the same but shorter, because there is no loan document to record alongside the deed.

Pinal County housing context

The county counts 539,380 residents, up from 425,264 in 2020. Owner-occupied homes make up 81.7 percent of housing, and the median owner-occupied value is $349,000 for 2020 to 2024. With that much growth, the Recorder's offices handle a steady flow of transfers.

Frequently asked questions

How much does Pinal County charge to record a deed?

$30 per document, or $15 for recordings requested by government bodies. The fee includes the affidavit of property value, indexing and the storage surcharge, plus $1 for mailing the document back. Plats and survey maps run $24 for the first sheet.

Where is the Pinal County Recorder's main office?

31 N Pinal Street, Building E, Florence, AZ 85132. Branch offices operate in Apache Junction, Casa Grande, Maricopa and San Tan Valley. All are open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Mail goes to P.O. Box 848, Florence, AZ 85132.

Can I record a deed in Pinal County by mail or online?

Yes. Mail the original with a check or money order, or record electronically through a trusted e-recording partner. Call any Recorder office for the partner list.

Do I need to file an affidavit of property value?

Yes, unless the transfer is exempt under A.R.S. 11-1134. Buyers and sellers must complete it, and skipping it is a class 2 misdemeanor. For an exempt transfer, write the statute and exemption code on the face of the deed instead.

Can the Pinal County Recorder prepare my deed or notarize it?

No. The office offers no notary service and can't give legal advice or help with documents. Have an attorney, title company or escrow officer prepare the deed and arrange the notary.

Everything recorded in Mohave County, from deeds and mortgages to liens, releases, affidavits and plats, goes through the Recorder. The main office is at 700 West Beale Street in Kingman, phone (928) 753-0701. Mail goes to P.O. Box 7000, Kingman, AZ 86402. All offices close on observed holidays.

The county stretches across 13,461 square miles of northwest Arizona, so the Recorder keeps three counters. A seller in Bullhead City or Lake Havasu City doesn't need to drive to the county seat.

  • Kingman (main office): 700 West Beale Street, (928) 753-0701, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Nothing on the Recorder's schedule rises with the sale price. Arizona's constitution (Article 9, Section 24) forbids the state, counties and cities from adding a tax, fee or stamp requirement on selling real property, and only charges in place on December 31, 2007 remain.

What you do get is paperwork. Under A.R.S. 11-1133, a deed that transfers title carries an Affidavit of Property Value, signed by both sides or their agents. Transfers that skip the affidavit

The exempt transfers are listed in A.R.S. 11-1134, and whichever exemption you rely on must be written on the face of the deed. A few come up often when a family is settling an estate or a divorce.

  • Moves into or out of a trust for token consideration, whether person to trustee or trustee to beneficiary.
  • Corrective deeds that confirm or fix one already on record.

A regular sale, cash buyer or not, fits none of these and needs the full affidavit. Doubtful about an exemption? Put the question to the closing title company first.

A signed, notarized original can be brought to any of the three counters. Mailing is the other option, with the fee enclosed, to the Kingman post office box (P.O. Box 7000, ZIP 86402). Staff test the document against A.R.S. 11-480, assign a recording number and make it permanent record. Walk-ins leave with the original after it is scanned. Mail takes roughly 4 to 6 weeks to come back. Indexers then enter the parties and parcel, which is what makes the deed searchable.

Once something is recorded, it stays on record, period. A faulty legal description or a misspelled name needs a second, corrective document and a second fee. Read the deed twice before handing it over.

A free Recorded Document Search sits on the Recorder's self-service site; type last name first in the both-name fields. Copies are $1.00 a page, ordered in person, online, by mail or on the phone at (928) 753-0701. To find the right record, give the book and page, the fee number, the recording date or the names on it. Include a stamped return envelope with a mailed request.

A clean search result isn't a guarantee the property is free of liens. Title insurance is what protects you. After the deed is recorded

The Recorder passes recorded documents to the Assessor, who changes the owner on the tax roll. More than 200 recorded documents reach the Assessor every day, so ownership updates move through a queue. Recording a legal document is the only way to change the owner name on real property.

If you still receive a tax bill after closing, forward it to the new owner or mail it to P.O. Box 712, Kingman, AZ 86402 with a note that the property was sold. Tax amounts, due dates and appeals are in the Mohave County property tax guide.

One order of events works well. Sign the deed and affidavit at the title company, let the title company record them, then ask for the recorded copy and keep it. A cash buyer's closing follows the same order, but with no lender there is no new deed of trust to record behind yours.

May I mail my deed to the Mohave County Recorder?

Yes. Send the original to P.O. Box 7000, Kingman, AZ 86402 with the correct fee. It is scanned and sent back to your return address, usually in 4 to 6 weeks.

Will the Mohave County Recorder tell me whose name goes on my deed?

No, because that is legal advice. Staff refer you to an attorney, title company or paralegal. They can explain how to search records and submit a document.

Recording fees

Every instrument costs one flat $30.00. Inside that price are the affidavit of property value, added indexing, the state surcharge and postage for the return trip, so you will not see a pile of extra line items on a typical deed. The recording fee increase rests on A.R.S. 11-475.

Gather these details before the signing, since the form wants every one of them:

  • An address for future tax statements.

  • Total price, any cash down payment, and how the purchase is financed: cash, a new third-party loan, a seller loan, an assumption, or an exchange.

Format rules that get a document rejected

Section 11-480 of the state code limits when a recorder may refuse a paper at the counter, and the list is short. The instrument needs a caption naming what it is, for example warranty deed. It has to be an original, signed in original ink, legible enough to copy, no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches, with type no smaller than ten point.

Leave two inches blank at the top of page one for the recording stamp, and keep every other margin at half an inch or more. A first page that misses the top margin can be fixed with a cover sheet carrying the title. If your paper amends one already on record, it must cite the earlier recording date and its docket and page.

Once the recorder accepts the paper, a later claim that it broke these rules does not invalidate it.

Selling for cash removes the lender from the picture. There is no buyer's mortgage to wait for, so fewer papers need to be matched and recorded, and the deed of trust that would normally follow your deed never appears. You still need the same core items: a deed with original signatures, an affidavit of legal value or exemption, a tax payoff from the Treasurer, and the recording fee. No larger than 8.5 by 14 inches, with type of at least ten point, a two inch top margin on page one and half inch margins elsewhere. A cover sheet can rescue a first page that comes up short.

Bring or send the deed to the Recorder's Office, 298 S. Main Street in Yuma (ZIP 85364). The counter opens at 8:00 a.m. and closes at 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday, and you can reach staff at (928) 373-6020. The Recorder keeps the county's public record and also runs voter registration and early voting. Deeds do not go to the Assessor or the Treasurer, who share a separate building at 197 S. Main Street. Think of the three offices this way: the Recorder files the paper, the Assessor tracks parcel values and ownership, and the Treasurer sends the tax bill and takes payment.

You can file in person, by mail or electronically. Title and escrow companies nearly always record electronically. Private owners handling their own paperwork usually walk the paper deed to the counter.

Any deed that moves title needs an Affidavit of Real Property Value. A.R.S. 11-1133 is the rule. Either party, or an agent acting for one of them, certifies the facts on a Department of Revenue form. The Assessor later reads these forms to update the parcel record, which is why they ask so much:

A cash sale has no lender paperwork, but the deed, the affidavit and the tax payoff still have to be in order. Recording works the same way whoever the buyer is, and it is the step that makes the new owner official in the public record.

Most Yuma sales follow the same rhythm. If you sell on your own, you carry more of these steps yourself: the signing, the affidavit, the trip or envelope to the Recorder and the tax payoff. None of them is hard, but each has a form or a fee attached, which is why a short phone call to the office beforehand pays off.

If the deed gets rejected

Recorders turn away documents for ordinary reasons: a missing affidavit, an exemption that is not written on the deed, a check made out to the wrong payee, or a mailing package without a return address. The Recorder's FAQ has an entry on the most common rejection reasons, so read it before you file, or phone the counter and ask what trips people up.

  2. The microfilm department films and scans the document.
  3. The original is mailed to the return address you typed on it.

Mailed originals take 15 to 20 business days to return. On an ordinary sale, escrow handles all of this, so ask your officer for the recording date instead of waiting on the mailbox.

Expect to supply quite a bit:

A single office, the Santa Cruz County Recorder, handles recording countywide. Deeds, mortgages, maps and surveys all pass through it, and voter registration lives there too. What a deed must look like

Arizona spells out the format in ARS 11-480. A document that misses one of the listed conditions can be turned away at the counter, so run through this list before sending anything.

If you want the recorded original mailed back, a return address fits in the left three and one-half inches of that top strip. The Recorder also points filers to the exemption codes in ARS 11-1134.

Affidavit of legal value and exempt deeds

A deed moving title, or a sales contract, has to come with an affidavit of legal value. Buyer and seller sign it, or an agent signs for them. The form, built on ARS 11-1133, asks for both parties' names and addresses, the legal description and parcel number, and the date of sale. Office location and hours

You will find the Graham County Recorder upstairs in the General Services Building, 921 Thatcher Boulevard, Safford, AZ 85546. The counter is staffed Monday to Thursday from 7 a.m. until 6 p.m. and closed on holidays. Friday is e-recording only, accepted until 5 p.m.

  • Phone: 928-428-3560.
  • Toll free: 888-428-3252.
  • Fax: 928-428-8828.
  • Mail: P.O. Box 747, Safford, AZ 85548.

Two jobs fall to this office: keeping property records and keeping voter registration records. A seller meets the first one whenever a deed, a deed of trust release or another paper must become part of the public record, nearly always by way of the title or escrow company.

Form rules a deed must meet

Arizona's A.R.S. 11-480 sets the layout tests, and a paper that fails any of them can be rejected at the counter. Graham County's own recording requirements repeat the same list.

RequirementRule
CaptionA heading that says in a few words what the document is
Original and legibleAn original or certified copy that is clear enough to copy again
SignaturesSigned in original ink unless the law says otherwise
Size and printPaper no bigger than 8.5 by 14 inches, with type of at least 10 point
MarginsHalf an inch at the sides and bottom, and 2 inches at the top of page one
Changes to an earlier documentName the recording date and the docket and page or sequence number being modified

Page one's top margin is held for the recording stamp. The left three and one-half inches can hold the name and return address of whoever requests the recording. The office supplies no forms, so get them at an office supply store or from a title company, and do not expect legal advice from staff, who follow instructions from the Graham County Attorney.

Do you need an Affidavit of Property Value?

Usually yes. The affidavit comes from A.R.S. 11-1133, which attaches it to every deed that moves title and to any sale contract for real property, with buyer and seller (or agents) signing. Submit a deed with a gap in the affidavit and no exemption noted, and the Recorder has to turn it down.

The affidavit collects:

  • Contact details for both sides, and where the tax statement should be sent.
  • Legal description, situs address and assessor's parcel number.
  • Sale date and total consideration, split into down payment and type of financing.
  • How the parties are related, and whether the home will be lived in by the owner or rented out.

Exempt transfers skip the affidavit but must name the exemption on the deed itself. The list in A.R.S. 11-1134 includes gifts, quitclaim deeds given for nothing, court-ordered conveyances, and token-price transfers among spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, or siblings. In this county the Arizona Department of Revenue exemption number has to accompany an exempt deed at recording. If an affidavit is absent or incomplete, the deed comes back to the sender.

Recording costs and transfer tax

The base charge is $30 per instrument under A.R.S. 11-475. A government party that requests the recording, whether the United States, the state or a political subdivision, pays $15. Both numbers already contain the amount charged under section 11-475.01.

Statute also prices copies: each page of a certified copy is $1, and the recorder's certificate and seal adds $3. The county posts its fees on a Recording Information page. For a long document or one needing extra indexing, phone the Recorder and ask for the total.

Is there a transfer tax? The Arizona Constitution, in Article 9, Section 24, forbids new taxes, fees and stamp requirements on conveying real property interests. Charges that already existed on December 31, 2007 are the exception. Ask the title company to show every recording charge on your settlement statement before you sign.

Recording electronically and searching records

Electronic filing in Graham County runs through a digital recording account and a published list of e-recording providers, and on a sale the title company usually submits for you. The Recorder's web page also lets anyone search recorded documents, which is handy for checking a prior deed or lien before you list.

A free Recording Notification service is available too. It monitors documents recorded with the office and alerts subscribers when something is filed. It helps an owner spot a recording that does not belong on the property, such as a fraudulent deed. If you get an alert and believe you are a fraud victim, the Recorder's page tells you to contact local law enforcement. The same page takes requests for copies of death certificates and military discharge (DD-214) forms.

Getting ready before the deed is recorded

Before the deed goes to Safford, it needs original signatures, correct margins and either a finished affidavit or an exemption code. The title company usually does this work, but you can double check it:

  • Compare the parcel number on the deed with the one printed on your tax bill.
  • Confirm that the whole legal description is there, since the affidavit asks for it.
  • Ask how the deed will arrive, by mail, in person or electronically, and when you can expect the recording number.
  • Save the recording number. If the original is ever lost, it lets you order a certified copy.

Taxes follow a different path. The Treasurer, at 928-428-3440, can tell you what is owed on the parcel, and statements typically show up in the new owner's name roughly a year after recording.

Titled mobile homes are handled differently. The county bills them as personal property and changes the tax record only after the buyer receives a new title. Signing the back of the old title will not move the roll, so finish the title transfer in addition to the deed.

Timing a visit to Safford

Because the counter closes on Fridays and stays open late Monday to Thursday, plan any in-person trip around those hours. Mail goes to the post office box, not the street address, so use P.O. Box 747 if you are sending anything by mail. If you hold a deed and need it recorded quickly, ask the title company whether it has a digital recording account, since an electronic filing can be accepted on a Friday when the counter is closed.

What a cash sale skips

A cash buyer needs no new loan, so the lender's title demands and the deed of trust that would otherwise trail your deed into the Recorder's office never come up. You still owe the basics: a signed deed, an affidavit or exemption, and a settled tax balance. Fewer parties means fewer places for the recording step to stall, and you can ask escrow to confirm the filing date once the deed is submitted. Keep the recording number with your closing file in case you need a certified copy later.

Graham County in brief

Safford serves as both seat and largest city of Graham County, a 4,641 square mile stretch of southeastern Arizona. As of 2025 it counts 40,157 residents and 14,645 housing units, with owners living in 73.1 percent of occupied homes. The median owner-occupied home was valued at $212,000 for 2020 through 2024 and median gross rent was $935. The county grew 4.2 percent between April 2020 and July 2025.

Frequently asked questions

What does it cost to record a deed in Graham County?

The basic charge is $30 per instrument, dropping to $15 for a government requester. Phone 928-428-3560 for the total on a lengthy document.

When is the Graham County Recorder open?

The counter opens Monday to Thursday, 7 a.m. to 6 p.m., except holidays, and e-recordings are taken until 5 p.m. on Fridays.

Is an Affidavit of Property Value required in Graham County?

In nearly every case, yes. Only transfers exempt under A.R.S. 11-1134 skip it, and a deed lacking a complete affidavit is returned unrecorded.

Will the Recorder help me prepare my deed?

No. Staff provide no forms and no legal advice, so turn to a title company or attorney. Blank forms are sold at office supply stores.

Does Graham County charge a transfer tax?

No new one can be created, since the Arizona Constitution bars fresh taxes or fees on conveying real property. Only charges that existed on December 31, 2007 survive, so ask your title company to itemize everything before you sign.
